title: Thorn's Spotlight matches a missing child's NCMEC photo to online sex ads; Thorn says she was recovered within weeks
summary: In April 2019 a California officer ran a NCMEC missing-child photo through Thorn's Spotlight; Rekognition matching returned sex ads with the girl and, per Thorn's CEO, she was recovered within weeks.
account: The date is WIRED's publication; the source places the case in April 2019 without a day. According to Thorn CEO Julie Cordua, speaking at an Amazon conference and quoted by WIRED's Tom Simonite, a California law enforcement officer saw a National Center for Missing and Exploited Children post with a missing child's picture, screenshotted it and ran it through Spotlight, Thorn's investigator tool that matches faces and other clues in online sex ads. Using Amazon's facial recognition, Spotlight returned a list of ads featuring the girl, who had been sold for weeks; more traditional police work followed and, Cordua said, the child was recovered within weeks. Snopes notes Thorn's 2017 impact report claimed its tools helped identify 5,791 child victims and rescue 103, figures from Thorn's surveys of police users, and that viral claims conflated identification with rescue. No police or court record of this case was fetched.
purpose: Help law-enforcement investigators find underage sex-trafficking victims by matching faces and text across online escort advertisements.
developer: Thorn (with Amazon Rekognition for face matching)
deployer: An unnamed California law enforcement officer and agency
taxonomy_note: The only account of the case is the maker's CEO as quoted by an independent journalist; the officer, agency and child are unnamed and no official record was fetched.

ratings.reason: A child sold for weeks was recovered and removed from trauma, per Thorn's CEO; no independent confirmation of the recovery was fetched.

ai_role.statement: The face match that surfaced the ads is attributed to Amazon Rekognition inside Spotlight; the recovery itself came from conventional police work. Everything about this case rests on Thorn's CEO, and Snopes documents that Thorn's aggregate figures derive from user surveys and were widely misreported, so the record is admitted only under the relaxed rule.

evidence.title: How Facial Recognition Is Fighting Child Sex Trafficking
evidence.quote: Using Amazon’s facial recognition technology, Spotlight quickly returned a list of online sex ads featuring the girl’s photo.

evidence.citation: Dan MacGuill, Snopes fact check, 4 Sep 2018
evidence.title: Did Ashton Kutcher's Software Help Rescue 6,000 Children from Sex Trafficking?
evidence.quote: As stated by Thorn themselves, the organization's digital tools had helped identify -- not rescue -- almost 6,000 child victims, a distinction that has sometimes been overlooked.
